Śrīcakra
------------------------------------------
The श्रीचक्र is perhaps, the most important and the most widely used symbol of the शक्ति cult, the cult of the votaries of the Divine मोथेर्. If God can be conceived of as the ड़थेर् in हेअवेन्, He can as well be conceived of as the मोथेर् Divine also. Though God is neither masculine nor feminine, human nature being what it is, it is but natural that anthropomorphic ways of worship are resorted to in religion. Once this principle is accepted, what form of the Deity can be more fitting for worship and contemplation than that of the all-loving Divine मोथेर्?
Even though मोथेर्-worship is very ancient in हिन्दुइस्म्, the ‘Father’ has not been neglected! In fact, the ड़थेर्-मोथेर्-Principle is one and the same. Just as fire and its burning power or the word and its meaning cannot be separated, even so शिव and शक्ति cannot be separated.
Though the three consorts of the Trinity—Sarasvatī of ब्रह्मा the creator, लक्ष्मी of विष्णु the protector and पार्वती of महेश्वर, the destroyer—are the main deities in the मोथेर्-cult, it is the various aspects of पार्वती that are most widely used in worship, जप or contemplation. In fact, an entire branch of Hindu religious practice, the तन्त्रस्, has developed round this Deity.
Again, दुर्गा, Kālī and ललिता are the three forms of पार्वती which are most widely used for worship. The श्रीचक्र is the symbol of the ललिता-aspect of the Divine मोथेर्. It is essentially a यन्त्र, a geometrical diagram representing the form-pattern of the Goddess.
The श्रीचक्र consists of a dot (bindu) at the centre surrounded by nine triangles (trikoṇa), of which five have their apexes downward and the other four, upward. The mutual intersections of these nine triangles form forty-three triangles in all. This is surrounded by two concentric circles with eight lotus petals and sixteen lotus petals. This again is surrounded by three more concentric circles. Finally on the outskirts, there is a square (caturasra) or three lines, the lines one inside the other, opening out in the middle of each side as four portals.
According to the Śāktatantras, scriptures of the cult of मोथेर् worship, the ultimate Reality is one, a transcendental Absolute which is immutable and ineffable. It is pictured as Supreme Effulgence, Prakāśa. Desiring to become many, this Absolute starts reflecting on Itself. This deliberation is technically designated विमर्श. This विमर्श creates a throb or stir, स्पन्द, which develops as vibration or नाद and gets concentrated to a point or बिन्दु.
This बिन्दु, like a dicotyledonous seed, contains the शिव-शक्ति principle as one closely-knit unit. It then gradually swells, giving rise to the polarisation of शिव (father-principle) and शक्ति (mother-principle), retaining simultaneously the original latent and potent status containing the शिव-शक्ति combination. These three units now form a triangle, as it were. This process goes on, until it results in the श्रीचक्र. This is nothing but a representation of the Supreme चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in its various levels of evolution.
We thus see that the श्रीचक्र is a symbol of the Divine, its ovulation into the created universe as well as the universe itself. In other words, it represents the Absolute in all its aspects.
The श्रीचक्र can be used for permanent worship, either in the form of a यन्त्र (two-dimensional engraved figure) or a मेरु (three-dimensional embossed figure). The यन्त्र can be drawn on a Bhūrja leaf, or plates of copper, silver or gold. The most common material for the मेरु is the pañcaloha (alloy of five metals—gold, silver, copper, tin and lead).

Śrīnivāsa
(‘the abode of Śrī [Lakṣmī or goddess of wealth]’)
------------------------------------------
This is another name of the famous deity वेङ्कटेश of तिरुमल-तिरुपति temple.
See TIRUPATI and VEṄKAṬEŚA.

------------------------------------------
The भक्ति Movement of Karnataka has been nourished and sustained by two traditions: the Śaiva tradition of the Śivaśaraṇas and the Vaiṣṇava tradition of the Haridāsas.
The latter is divided into two parallel but closely knit streams—the vyāsakūṭa and the दासकूट. (See DĀSAKŪṬA.) The vyāsakūṭa comprises the saṁnyāsins of the Mādhva sect whereas the दासकूट consists of the householders, also of the same sect.
Śrīpādarāja was a pioneer of the vyāsakūṭa.
Known as Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa (the son of Śeṣagiri and Giriyamma) in his premonastic days, he was adopted by Svarṇa-varṇatīrtha, the abbot of a द्वैत monastery at Muḷabāgilu (Mulbagal, in the Kolar district of Karnataka). After initiation into the monastic order, he was given the name Lakṣmīnārāyaṇayogi. Later on he came to be popularly known as श्रीपादराज or Śrīpādarāyaru. Under his गुरु’s vigorous training he became a great scholar and a monk of repute.
After taking over as the abbot of the monastery, when his teacher passed away, he worked hard to improve its condition and expand its scope as also the area of its influence.
Sāḷuva Narasiṁharāja, who was the king of a small state Candragiri, became his disciple in A.

, and was greatly benefited by his holy influence.
Śrīpādarāya then undertook a long पिल्ग्रिमगे to काशी and other places, establishing his reputation as an invincible scholar.
After returning to his place, he started the new tradition of introducing bhajans and saṅkīrtans (devotional hymns and songs) in Kannada, the local language of the people, in his monastery, especially after ritualistic worship. This gave the common people a grand opportunity to understand the essence of the Sanskrit scriptures in their own language.
There are several Kannada compositions attributed to him.
He is reputed to have exhibited many miraculous powers including the rising of the गङ्गा-waters at the pond known as the Nṛsiṁhatīrtha near the monastery.
He passed away in A.

Śrīkaṇṭha
------------------------------------------
Śrīkaṇṭha is one of the important ācāryas who have written commentaries on the Brahmasūtras. He advocates a type of शैविस्म् as contained in the Vāyavīya-saṁhitā of the Śivapurāṇa.
According to him ब्रह्मन् is शिव (Saguṇa-ब्रह्मन्). प्रकृति (nature) and jīvas (individual souls who are atomic in size) are his parts as it were. Evolution of the world takes place as per his will and supervision. Though, thus, he is the निमित्तकारण or the efficient cause, he is, in a way, the उपादानकारण or the material cause also since प्रकृति is his part.
Śrīkaṇṭha considers that the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and the prescribed duties without any selfish motive, prepares a person for the realisation of शिव.
Man (or the सोउल्) is free to do good or bad as per his सṁस्कारस् carried over from the previous lives. However, शिव the merciful, is ever eager to help him to do good and get लिबेरतिओन्.
The souls are the conscious knowers, both by way of the senses and by the मनस् (superior मिन्द्, which is a special property possessed by them, different from the ordinary मिन्द् which is a product of प्रकृति). By following the path of ज्ञानयोग, the threefold impurities of the मिन्द् (See MALA for details.) are removed and self-knowledge is fully manifested. It is almost like the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्.
In the state of लिबेरतिओन्, the सोउल् has no body but enjoys bliss through the मिन्द्. If it wants, it can also create its own body and enjoy all happiness. It is never again brought under the control of कर्म.
Śrīkaṇṭha’s philosophy may be termed as Śivaviśiṣṭādvaita, because of its similarity to Rāmānuja’s system.
Appayya Dīkṣita (A.

-1592) has written an excellent commentary called Śivārkamaṇidīpikā on the bhāṣya of श्रीकण्ठ.
It is not known when exactly श्रीकण्ठ lived. Some scholars suggest that he lived in A.

Śrīharṣa
------------------------------------------
One of the few important dialecticians of Advaita Vedānta, श्रीहर्ष probably lived during the middle part of the 12th century A. D., in the court of the king Jayacandra of Kanyākubja (Kanauj).
Naiṣadhacarita, a great poetical work describing the story of नल and दमयन्ती and Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya, a highly polemical work attacking the न्याय school of philosophy are his two most well known works. Nine more works like Arṇava-Varṇana, Vijaya-praśasti and Īśvarābhisandhi are also attributed to him.
See also KHAṆḌANA-KHAṆḌA-KHĀDYA.

Śrīkarabhāṣya
------------------------------------------
The Śrīkarabhāṣya is the magnum opus of Śrīpatipaṇḍita.
The Brahmasūtras is a basic work of Vedānta. Among the several ācāryas who have written commentaries on it, Śrīpatipaṇḍita is also one. He most probably lived in the 14th century A. D. He was a saṁnyāsin belonging to one of the five famous monasteries, the Ekorāma मठ situated at Kedāra in the हिमालयस्. He was supposed to have been born with a part of the divine power of Nārayaṇa (Nārāyaṇāṁśasambhūta). Apart from being a great scholar he also had miraculous powers. He might have lived in the area near Vijayavada of the modern Andhra Pradesh.
He was a Vīraśaiva and hence his bhāṣya reflects the philosophy of that sect. He declares that he has followed the Vṛtti (brief commentary) of Agastyamuni. However, this work has not been traced till now. He adores Revaṇa, Maruḷa and राम, earlier teachers of his school.
His philosophy in which the पूर्वमीमाṁसा and the Vedānta are taken as forming one science, and based mainly on this bhāṣya, may be summarised as follows:
Brahman who is शिव or Paraśiva is the only reality. His existence can be proved only by the Śrutis (Vedas, उपनिषद्स् and the Bhagavadgītā). He is a person without any particular form but with infinite knowledge and power (nirākāra and saguṇa). Māyā is this power.
Before च्रेअतिओन्, प्रकृति or matter (which is in the परमाणु or atomic state) and the jīvas (souls) are inherent in him. He creates the universe out of himself as per the कर्म of the individuals. In one sense, he is the efficient cause and in another the material cause also.
The world is real and not an इल्लुसिओन्.
The jīvas are aṁśas or parts of ब्रह्मन्. Hence they are similar to him in nature. They are eternal and are aṇu (atomic) in character. Their number is infinite. They have the capacity for understanding and also the power to act independently.
By performing the duties prescribed in the वेदस् in a desireless manner, the जीव becomes pure in heart. By meditating on ब्रह्मन् as शिव and worshipping him, the जीव attains him. Becoming like him (sārūpya) he lives in eternal bliss in Śivaloka which is the same as Brahma-लोक. He will never return to this world. He will continue to be obedient to शिव and serve him for ever.
Being a pioneer of Vīraśaiva philo-sophy, Śrīpatipaṇḍita supports the षट्स्थलसिद्धान्त and the wearing of the शिवलिङ्ग on the body.
See ŚAIVISM also.

Śrīvaiṣṇavism
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Śrīvaiṣṇavism, the religion, and Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, its philosophy, are of hoary antiquity. In his introductory verse of Śrībhāṣya (the commentary on the Brahma Sūtras), Śrī Rāmānuja traces this philosophy to the उपनिषद्स्, which was well guarded by the later Ācāryas like व्यास, बोधायन, टङ्क, Dramiḍa, Guhadeva, Kapardin, Bhāruci and others. According to the tradition that obtains among the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, the religion of श्रीवैष्णविस्म् was first taught by the Lord नारायण himself to लक्ष्मी, his divine Consort, who communicated the same to विष्वक्सेन. From him it was handed over to a series of teachers headed by Śaṭhagopa.
The Āḷvārs
Āḷvārs are श्रीवैष्णव saints of the Tamil country who lived between the sixth and the ninth centuries A. D. The word ‘Āḷvār’ literally means one who is immersed in divine love. They are twelve in number: Poygai, Pūdam, Pey, Tirumoḷiśai, नम्माऌवार्, Kulaśekhara, पेरियाऌवार्, Toṇḍaraḍippoḍi, Tirumaṅgai, Tiruppāṇ, Madhurakavi, and आण्डाऌ. Theirs was a religion of ecstatic love for God. Hence, neither caste nor sex was any barrier to their attaining to that state.
Coming to the historical times, it was these आऌवार्स् who first propagated the religion and the philosophy of श्रीवैष्णविस्म् through their songs. These songs, called the Nālāyira Prabandham, combine in themselves rare poetic beauty and high philosophical tenets, couched in a simple language.
Nammāḷvār, the author of the famous Tiruvāimoḷi, is by far the greatest among them. He is called the Kūṭastha by the later Ācāryas of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्, because the fundamental doctrines of this faith as current today, were taught by him.
The Ācāryās
The Āḷvār movement was more emotional in nature than metaphysical. The आऌवार्स् were great devotees of the Lord विष्णु. They believed in the impermanence of worldly enjoyments and in the acquisition of लिबेरतिओन् by union with Him. They taught more by example than by precept, though they propagated the philosophy of Viśiṣṭādvaita in their songs.
Hence it was left to the Ācāryas beginning with नाथमुनि, who succeeded the आऌवार्स्, to put the system on a firm footing, basing it both upon the Sanskrit scriptures and the Tamil teachings of the आऌवार्स्. The Ācāryas were very orthodox ब्राह्मणस्, well-versed equally in Sanskrit and Tamil, who passed through the different stages of orthodox life and discharged their duties so as to serve as an ideal for their followers. Apart from expounding the philosophy of Viśiṣṭādvaita, they also laid down various rules for the proper observance of festivals, fasts, vows and customs. They were thus the makers of modern श्रीवैष्णविस्म्. It is not surprising, therefore, that they in turn have become objects of worship like the आऌवार्स् whom they themselves apotheosized.
The first of the Ācāryas was Raṅganāthamuni, popularly known as नाथमुनि (A.

-924). He was at once an erudite scholar, a yogin, and a devotee. It was he who first collected all the Prabandhams, edited them with proper introductory verses, popularized them by setting them to मुसिच्, and made them sung in temples. It was, again, he who gave these Prabandhams the status equal to that of the वेदस् in temple festivals. The various reforms brought about by नाथमुनि necessitated the च्रेअतिओन् of a post of a universal आचार्य whose authority was law in religious worship and whose advice was a guide to temples and होउसे-holders. It was but natural that when such a post was established, the choice should fall on नाथमुनि himself. Since this office was combined with the management of the श्रीरङ्गम् temple, it was easy for the Ācāryas to revolutionize and reorganize the श्रीवैष्णव cult by introducing the necessary reforms first in that temple, which is one of the most important shrines of विष्णु and a stronghold of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्.
Nāthamuni was succeeded by Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Rāmamiśra for two short periods. Then came यामुनाचार्य (A.

-1038), who was the grandson of नाथमुनि himself. It was he who, endowed with great scholarship and insight, first attempted to put the Viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy on a firm foundation. He wrote scholarly works in Sanskrit defending it, and established the orthodoxy of the Pāñcarātra school, whose authority is accepted as equal to that of the Śrutis by the Viśiṣṭādvaitins. Siddhitraya and Āgamaprāmāṇya are his two important works, in addition to the Gītārtha-saṅgraha. It was his cherished desire to write a commentary on the Brahmasūtras according to the Viśiṣṭādvaita, just as शङ्कर had done according to the Advaita. But he died before he could attempt it, and it fell on Rāmānuja to achieve it.
Rāmānuja (A.

-1137)
The name of Rāmānuja is inseparably associated with the Viśiṣṭādvaita, just as शङ्कर’s is with the Advaita. The traditional date of his birth is A.

, and he is said to have lived for 120 years. Yāmuna died before Rāmānuja became the आचार्य, and the interval was filled up by Mahāpūrṇa.
Yāmuna bequeathed to Rāmānuja the three great tasks of his life which he himself had failed to achieve, viz., the perpetuation of the memory of the sage पराशर, the immortalization of the glory of नम्माऌवार्, and the interpretation of बादरायण’s Brahmasūtras according to the Viśiṣṭādvaita system. Rāmānuja fulfilled all these three in his lifetime. He commanded भट्ट, the son of कूरेश, to write a commentary on the Viṣṇusahasra-nāma, and named him as पराशर. He authorized कुरुकेश, the son of his uncle Śrīśailapūrṇa, to compose a commentary on the Tiruvāimoḷi of नम्माऌवार्.
To achieve the third object, Rāmānuja had to undertake an arduous journey to Kashmir, where the last surviving copy of the Vṛtti of बोधायन, a commentary on the Brahmasūtras was available. After going through it with great difficulty, he composed his Śrībhāṣya, a masterly commentary on the Brahmasūtras.
Rāmānuja was as great an organizer as he was a thinker. He divided the श्रीवैष्णव world into seventy-four Ācāryic dioceses, over each of which he appointed a pious householder as the head or ‘siṁhāsanādhipati’ as he was called. These spiritual leaders earnestly took up the work of carrying the message of Viśiṣṭādvaita to all the villages and homes, each within his diocese.
Split in श्रीवैष्णव Ranks
The demise of Rāmānuja was followed by a period of sectarian split among the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, which ultimately ended in the permanent division of their ranks into the two sects of वडगलैस् and Teṅgalais. These words literally mean the followers of the northern and the southern schools respectively. The two sects developed separate sets of works, separate lineage of gurus, and separate traditions in many matters of practical importance.
The language of the holy books to be studied, the comparative importance of भक्ति and प्रपत्ति (self-surrender) in the path of लिबेरतिओन्, relation with the lower castes, details of certain ceremonials to be observed on certain special occasions, and a few other questions were the causes for such a division. The वडगलैस् favoured the Sanskrit works and the path of भक्ति, and were more conservative in their relation towards the lower castes. The Teṅgalais, on the other hand, preferred the Tamil works to the Sanskrit ones, and laid greater stress on प्रपत्ति based on the mārjālakiśoranyāya (the maxim of the kitten totally dependent on its मोथेर्) than on the markaṭakiśora-nyāya (the maxim of the young one of the monkey which clings to its मोथेर्). The former assumes self-effort as a prerequisite to प्रपत्ति whereas the latter does not.
Though there has never been a check to interdining, intermarriage, and free social harmony at home or at the temple, the allegiance to different teachers and philosophies, as also the scramble for control over the temples, has perpetuated this division.
Apostolic Successors of Rāmānuja
The two sects have a different गुरु-paramparā (succession of teachers) though both trace their origin to Rāmānuja himself. कुरुकेश was the first successor of Rāmānuja according to the वडगलैस्. विष्णुचित्त, his successor, is the author of two famous works Sārārthacatuṣṭaya and Viṣṇucittīyam (a commentary on the Viṣṇupurāṇa). The next in line is Varadārya or Varadācārya, otherwise known as Naḍādūr Ammāḷ. A substance of his lectures and interpretations of the Śrībhāṣya was committed to writing under the title of Śrutaprakāśikā by a talented disciple of his, named सुदर्शनसूरि.
After the death of Varadārya, the Ācāryaship devolved on आत्रेय Rāmānuja, who in turn was succeeded by वेदान्त देशिक or Veṅkaṭanātha.
Vedānta Deśika (A.

-1370)
Vedānta Deśika, who was a contemporary of विद्यारण्य, is undoubtedly the greatest of the Ācāryās of the post Rāmānuja period. For more than three quarters of a century, he enriched the श्रीवैष्णव world with his teachings and writings. His works number more than a hundred, and are characterized by versatility, beauty of style and thought, and a deep spiritual insight. He was a poet, a philosopher, a thinker, a polemist, and a sage, all rolled into one. His works include original writings in Tamil, as also commentaries on older works. Gītābhāṣya-tātparyacandrikā, bhāṣya on the Īśā-vāsyopaniṣad, Tattvaṭīkā, अधिकरण-sārāvalī, Nyāyasiddhañjana, Saccaritra-rakṣā, रहस्यत्रयसार, and Haṁsa-sandeśa are only a few of the important works which may be mentioned here. It is not a matter of surprise that he was called in his own times as ‘Kavitārkika-siṁha.’ One of the greatest of his services was his saving the Śrutaprakāśikā from the chaos that followed in the wake of invasion of श्रीरङ्गम् by the Mohammedans. It is for this reason that his name as Vedāntācārya is gratefully remembered by all the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, without sectarian bias, in beginning the study of the Śrībhāṣya.
Piḷḷai लोकाचार्य (A.

-1327)
The तेङ्गलै sect traces the apostle ship in succession of Rāmānuja in the following manner: Embār, पराशर भट्ट, Nañjīyar (the famous commentator of the Prabandham), Nampillai, कृष्ण-pāda, पिऌऌऐ लोकाचार्य, Tirumalai Āḷvār, मणवाऌअ मामुनि (or वरवरमुनि). Among these, पिऌऌऐ लोकाचार्य, who was a contemporary of वेदान्त देशिक, occupies the same place amidst the Teṅgalais as Deśika does among the वडगलैस्. In fact, he is generally regarded as the founder of Teṅgalaism as a distinct sect. Being a man of brilliant intellect, he composed several treatises in order to uphold his school. Vacanabhūṣaṇa is a difficult work in aphoristic style which deals with the doctrine of प्रपत्ति in all its aspects. For the benefit of women and the common folk, लोकाचार्य composed sixteen treatises on the secret doctrines and the philosophy of श्रीवैष्णविस्म् like Nigamanappaḍi, Mumukṣuppaḍi, Tattvatraya, Arthapañcaka, etc. Though most of these works are small in size, they are regarded by the तेङ्गलै school as the only correct interpretation of the cults of Rāmānuja and the आऌवार्स्.
Maṇavāḷa Māmuni (A.

-1443)
Piḷḷai लोकाचार्य was succeeded by Śrīśaileśa, who in turn handed over the Ācāryaship to मणवाऌअ मामुनि, also known as Aḷagiya Maṇavāḷa or वरवरमुनि. He was a master of the Tamil Veda and other lore. Though he was trained by the teachers of the Vaḍagalai sect also, he openly declared that Īḍu (the commentary by Kṛṣṇapāda on the Tamil Veda) was the equal of Śrībhāṣya. He wrote several works explaining the treatises of पिऌऌऐ लोकाचार्य. Though his works were limited in range and diction, he gave a definite form to Teṅgalaism. His magnetic personality elevated him in the eyes of his followers to the position of an इन्चर्नतिओन् of Rāmānuja.
Śrīvaiṣṇavism in Practice
Everyone born in a श्रीवैष्णव family must approach a proper गुरु and undergo what is called pañcasaṁskāra, if he is to be considered a true श्रीवैष्णव. This five-fold ritual includes तपस् or the आचार्य’s initiating the student into the sacred fire by ब्रन्दिन्ग् the latter’s shoulders with the symbols of विष्णु; the पुण्ड्र or initiating into wearing the sectarian mark, the symbol of the Lord’s foot; giving a spiritual name like Nārāyaṇadāsa or Govindadāsa to the disciple; imparting the three mantras. viz., the aṣṭākṣarī, the dvaya, and the carama-śloka; and handing over a शालग्राम or other concrete objects for daily worship.
Though in theory this pañcasaṁskāra is enough to secure the devotee’s entry into the blissful world of Lord विष्णु, in practice he finds that his past कर्म and present weaknesses are serious obstacles to spiritual progress. He is thus forced to realise that the Lord’s grace is absolutely necessary, and therefore surrenders himself at his feet. This is technically called ‘prapatti’ or ‘śaraṇāgati,’ and the devotee who does it is known as a ‘prapanna.’
The prapanna is again, in need of a mediator, since he is unable to communicate with the Lord directly. Therefore, he has to go to a teacher and beg him to intercede on his behalf and place his सोउल् at the Lord’s feet. This vicarious employment of the teacher is technically designated as ‘bhāranyāsa.’
Śrīvaiṣṇava Maṭhas
The evolution and consolidation of श्रीवैष्णविस्म् as a cult is closely associated with the origin and development of the श्रीवैष्णव Maṭhas or monasteries. From the most ancient times, āśramas and maṭhas in India have been the repositories of religion in theory and practice. Their heads, whether मोन्क्स् or pious householders, have been responsible for arresting the decay of धर्म and for propagating true religion, apart from guiding the society often in secular matters also. The same holds good in the case of the श्रीवैष्णव Maṭhas too. अहोबिल मठ, परकाल मठ, Yadugiri Yatirāja मठ, आण्डवन् मठ and Vānamāmalai Maṭha—these are some of the important maṭhas of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्.
The अहोबिल मठ was founded in the year A.

, in the Ahobila Kshetra of Andhra Pradesh, by Śrīnivāsācārya, who became a saṁnyāsin under the name of Ādi Vaṇa Śaṭhagopa Svāmin. He was a great scholar and lived as a saṁnyāsin for the full length of sixty-years. The successive Jeers or abbots of the मठ have kept up the tradition of erudition and of touring the country to spread religion.
According to the tradition that obtains at the परकाल मठ in Mysore (Karnataka), its founder was वेदान्त देशिक himself. His disciple, Periya Brahmatantra Svatantra Svāmin, occupied the पीठ or pontifical seat in A.

. So far there have been thirty-three Jeers (abbots). The principal deity worshipped in the मठ is हयग्रीव, which has been handed down to the मठ from वेदान्त देशिक himself.
Yadugiri is a small hill, about 48 kms. (30 miles) to the east of Mysore. It is claimed that Rāmānuja himself established a मठ here during A.

. This मठ, known as Yadugiri Yatirāja मठ, had a branch at Rewa (in Madhya Pradesh), which is now functioning independently. Some of the Jeers of this मठ had kept contacts with North India also.
The आण्डवन् मठ, better known as “Śrīraṅgam Āṇḍavan आश्रम,” has its main centre at श्रीरङ्गम् in Tamil Nadu. Vedānta Rāmānuja Deśika is the founder of this मठ, the youngest among the श्रीवैष्णव Maṭhas. It was started in early nineteenth century. The present head is the seventh in the apostolic succession.
Vānamāmalai मठ was established at Nangunderi, Tirunelveli District, Tamil Nadu, by मणवाऌअ मामुनि during the fourteenth century A. D. So far there have been twenty-seven Jeers.
The Philosophy of Viśiṣṭādvaita
Any account of the history of श्रीवैष्णविस्म् should be deemed incomplete without a description of its philosophical tenets. As has already been pointed out, this philosophy is much older than Rāmānuja, who only systematized it. However, the pioneering and yet stupendous work he has turned out in the cause of Viśiṣṭādvaita has justified its being called Rāmānuja दर्शन. Viśiṣṭādvaita is essentially a philosophy of religion. In it, reason and faith coalesce to become ‘reasoned faith.’ It is often identified with the older Seśvara Mīmāṁsā, and is also called Ubhaya Vedānta, since it accepts both the Sanskrit प्रस्थानत्रय and the Tamil Prabandham as equally authoritative. Pāñcarātra treatises are also put on a par with the वेदस्.
See VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA VEDANTA DARŚANA for details.
Conclusion
Thus श्रीवैष्णविस्म्, with its Philo-sophy of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta and the great stress laid on भक्ति and प्रपत्ति, has made the path of spiritual evolution a little more easy for the ordinary sādhakas or spiritual aspirants. It has also contributed to social harmony, at least among its own ranks.

Śrīpañcamī
------------------------------------------
Śrīpañcamī is one of the minor festivals of the Hindus. It is observed on the Mārgaśira-śukla-pañcamī day (the fifth day in the bright half of the month Mārgaśira, generally in November/ December).
It is a day sacred to Śrī or लक्ष्मी and is dedicated to her worship. The worship may be offered to a metallic or clay image or even to a picture. Honouring chaste married women and donating a cow to a worthy person are recommended.
The worship may also be carried on for one full year, observing it as a vrata (religious vow) on the śukla-pañcamī every lunar month.

Śrīdharasvāmin
------------------------------------------
Śrīdharasvāmin or Śrīdhara is one of the few commentators belonging to the Advaita school of Vedānta who has tried to harmonise ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion) in his writings.
He probably lived in the 15th century A. D. A ब्राह्मण from Maharashtra, he lived in Gujarat.
He was a householder and an apparently insignificant incident in his life made him renounce the world and become a saṁnyāsin.
His works are:
Subodhinī
(commentary on the Bhagavadgītā);
Bhāvārthadīpikā
(commentary on the Bhāgavata);
Ātmaprakāśa
(commentary on the Viṣṇupurāṇa);
His writings are quite popular among the students of Vedānta.

Śrīsūkta
(‘hymn devoted to Śrī [or लक्ष्मी]’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. They are defined as those sacred texts which can show the human beings divine means of getting what they want and getting rid of what they do not want.
A सूक्त is a Vedic hymn devoted to a particular devatā or deity.
Some of the well-known sūktas which are commonly used in religious rituals even today are: Agnisūkta, Bhūsūkta, Devīsūkta, Medhāsūkta, Nārāyaṇasūkta, Nīḷāsūkta, Puruṣasūkta, Śrīsūkta and Viṣṇusūkta.
Out of these the Puruṣasūkta and the Śrīsūkta are much more popular and in constant use.
The Śrīsūkta is the खिल part of the Ṛgveda appearing after the 5th मण्डल. Those mantras of the वेदस् for which no viniyoga (utility) has been mentioned in the Kalpasūtras, are technically called ‘khila’. (See also KHILA.)
The Śrīsūkta contains 15 ṛks, the 16th stating its use and utility in rituals.
Since it has been considered extremely important, several commentaries have been written on the same by competent scholars from different angles. Some of them are: Āṇḍavallīvyākhyāna, Bhāgadheyabhūṣaṇam, Cidvilāsavṛtti, Pṛthvīdharabhāṣya, Sārasvatasiddhi, Śatānandavṛtti, Saubhāgyasañjīvanam, Sāyaṇabhāṣya, Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya, Śrīsūkta-bhāṣya (by Nañjīyar) and Sūktārtha-saṅgraha.
While these are direct commentaries on the Śrīsūkta itself, there are other works where some of the verses are referred to and explained, mostly from the practical aspects of worship. They are: Mahālakṣmīratnakośa, Mantrakalpārṇava and Śrīvidyāvilāsa. They provide icono-graphic details, methods of drawing yantras (mystic diagrams), prescriptions for पूजा (worship), जप (recitation) and होम (oblations).
Though a part of the Ṛgveda, the Śrīsūkta has been given an independent status. Its ṛṣi (seer) is इन्द्र or लक्ष्मी herself or her four sons—Ānanda, कर्दम, Ciklīta and Śrīda or Indirāsuta. The devatā (deity) is Śrī (Lakṣmī). Or, Śrī and Jātavedas (Agni, god of fire) can be the deities. ‘Jātavedas’ is sometimes interpreted as नारायण also. The छन्दस् (Vedic metre) is varied:
ślokas 1 to 3 are in anuṣṭubh.
śloka 4 is in बृहती.
ślokas 5 and 6 are in triṣṭubh.
ślokas 5 to 14 are in anuṣṭubh.
śloka 15 is in prastārapaṅkti.
The viniyoga (utility) is to get the grace of महालक्ष्मी as also dispelling the evil effects of अलक्ष्मी (the deity of misfortune).
The dhyānaśloka (hymn for contemplation) (amalakamalasaṁsthā etc.) describes her form thus: ‘She is seated on a pure lotus. Her colour resembles that of the dust of the lotus. In her two hands she is holding two lotuses whereas the other two hands are exhibiting the gestures of boon-giving (varada) and protection (abhīti or fearlessness). There is a resplendent jewel-studded crown on her head. She is wearing a garland of lotus flowers. May this Goddess, the मोथेर् of the universe, bring prosperity to us always!’
Sometimes करन्यास and अङ्गन्यास (ritual placements of divine powers on one’s limbs) are also given before the dhyānaśloka.
The ritualistic preliminaries given here are for the whole hymn.
Such processes have been described by the commentators separately for each of the verses also.
Similarly a यन्त्र (mystical diagram for worship or wearing on the body) for the whole hymn and separate individual ones for each of the verses have also been prescribed.
Now a summary of the whole सूक्त can be attempted:
Verse 1
O all knowing अग्नि! Please bring unto me the goddess of good-fortune, who is of golden complexion, who is bright, who is wearing a garland of flowers made of gold and silver, who like the मोओन्, is bringing joy and who is golden.
Verse 2
O all-knowing अग्नि! Bring to me that लक्ष्मी (the goddess of wealth and well-being) who will never leave me and on whose arrival I will be able to possess gold, cows, horses, sons, grandsons as also servants.
Verse 3
As the procession of the मोथेर्-goddess draws near, with horses ahead and chariots in the centre, her arrival is proclaimed by the roar of the elephants. I beseech the goddess to come near me. May she be gracious unto me!
Verse 4
I invoke that goddess who is ब्रह्मन् the Absolute! She is smiling. She is of the form of gold. She is cool, but brilliant. She is ever content, but satisfies the desires of the devotees. She is seated on a lotus and is of the same colour as that of the lotus.
Verse 5
I take refuge in this goddess who is delightful like the मोओन्, effulgent, shining in all the worlds due to renowned qualities, who is being served by gods (like इन्द्र), who is generous, who is holding lotuses in her hands and who is designated by the letter ‘īm’. I seek your protection for the destruction of misfortune.
Verse 6
O goddess who is brilliant like the sun! By your grace, the बिल्व tree (Aegle marmelos) belonging to the vanaspati group (trees that produce fruits without flowering) was produced. It was then that its fruits attained celebrity by your grace. May they dispel the veil of इग्नोरन्चे inside and destroy the misfortunes outside!
Verse 7
May god कुबेर, the friend of महादेव (Śiva) along with fame (or the goddess of fame) and the jewel called चिन्तामणि, come to me. Since I have been born in this world of men, may he (Kubera) grant me celebrity and prosperity.
Verse 8
O goddess Śrī! I will destroy or drive away that deity of misfortune (called अलक्ष्मी) who comes in the form of hunger and thirst. Please drive away all poverty and lack of prosperity from my होउसे.
Verse 9
I invoke the presence here of Śrī, the goddess of prosperity, who is verily Bhū or the earth endowed with a peculiar aroma, who is hard to damage, who is ever well-nourished, who has an abundance of cattle and who is the ruler of all living beings.
Verse 10
May I obtain by your grace, the desires of the मिन्द्, happiness, truthful speech, wealth of cattle, abundant ड़ोओद् and good name. May लक्ष्मी, who is capable of all this, come to me.
Verse 11
O कर्दम! The goddess Śrī has you for her son. Hence, kindly show your grace to me by making your मोथेर्, the wearer of a garland of lotuses, reside in my abode.
Verse 12
May the deities presiding over the element water generate amiable effects for me! O Ciklīta! Come and dwell in my होउसे. And, make thy मोथेर्, the goddess of wealth and prosperity, to live in my household.
Verse 13
O अग्नि! Bring unto me, लक्ष्मी, who is moist with compassion. She is being bathed by two elephants. She is nourishing the worlds of yellow hue, she is wearing a garland of lotuses. She is of pleasant complexion like the मोओन्. She is bedecked with golden ornaments. (Bring her unto me!)
Verse 14
O अग्नि! Bring unto me लक्ष्मी, the goddess who is cool, who is holding the mace of righteousness, who is lustrous like gold, who is wearing a garland of golden flowers, who is brilliant like the sun and who is bedecked with golden ornaments.
Verse 15
O अग्नि! Please bring unto me that लक्ष्मी who will never go away from my home, by whose presence I will be able to obtain abundant wealth, cattle, maids, horses, relatives and well-wishers—like sons, friends and others.
There is a sixteenth मन्त्र mentioned in the Nirukta of यास्क, which gives the phalaśruti, what one gets if he uses the hymn in the prescribed ritualistic manner.
It is customary to chant another 18 ślokas after reciting the Śrīsūkta. They are in simple classical Sanskrit and form a long hymn.
Besides this well-known Śrīsūkta, there is another, known as the Kashmir recension. It comprises 31 verses divided into five groups.
As mentioned earlier each of the 15 verses has separate ritualistic usage, the prescriptions being quite difficult and complicated.
The work Mantrakalpārṇava gives all the details of religious observances. The results projected may be summarised as follows:
Verse 1
Wealth, health and long-life.
Verse 2
Plenty of wealth in the form of gold, cows, sons and grandsons.
Verse 3
If observed by a king, he will become invincible and attain great wealth.
Verse 4
Destruction of poverty and all types of wants.
Verse 5
Attainment of wealth, honour by the king, victory in battles, going to the world of मोओन् after death.
Verse 6
Destruction of sorrow and suffering.
Verse 7
Vision of deities like कुबेर, securing many kinds of gems and destruction of evil spirits.
Verse 8
Destruction of इग्नोरन्चे, sins, misfortune and diseases.
Verse 9
Increase of agricultural produce, cattle and wealth, name and fame, and power.
Verse 10
Perfection of speech, attainment of wealth and all kinds of enjoyments.
Verse 11
Continuity of the family lineage.
Verse 12
Attainment of various kinds of ड़ोओद् and other objects of enjoyment.
Verses 13 and 14
Obtaining emperorship, control over others, name and fame.
Verse 15
Victory over enemies, attainment of knowledge and wisdom as also kingship.
It is thus seen that this Śrīsūkta has become a potent means of sādhana for attaining लक्ष्मी’s grace, both here and hereafter.

Śrīraṅgam
------------------------------------------
Śrīraṅgam is one of the most sacred places of पिल्ग्रिमगे for the devotees of Viṣṇu—especially the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, the followers of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137)—ranking next only to तिरुपति (in Andhra Pradesh). This small town is situated just 5 kms. (3 miles) from the Tiruchirapalli railway station which itself is 320 kms. (200 miles) to the south-west of Chennai (Madras) in Tamil Nadu.
This little town, the whole of which is the temple-complex dedicated to रङ्गनाथ (an aspect of नारायण or विष्णु), is located on the island formed by the river कावेरी which splits into two streams—the कावेरी and the Kollaḍam—which later rejoin. The temple proper is known by several names such as Koil, Bhūvaikuṇṭha, Tiruvaraṅga-तिरुपति, Ādiraṅga and Bhogamaṇḍapa.
The chief deity is considered to be svayaṁvyakta (self-manifested) and not man-made. According to the local legends this deity has a very ancient history. Originally worshipped by ब्रह्मा, the creator, it was handed over to the kings of the इक्ष्वाकु race. Later on श्रीराम gave it to विभीषण to take it to लङ्का and establish it in a temple there. However, on his way to लङ्का, विभीषण had to place it on the ground at the time of his evening prayer. The image got firmly fixed on the ground (at the present place known as श्रीरङ्गम्) and विभीषण had to return empty-handed.
श्रीरङ्गम्">Temple Towers at Śrīraṅgam(However, there is a belief that he comes once in twelve years in the night, quietly worships it and goes back!)
From this legend this much can be assumed that the original shrine is very ancient. It must have been renovated and rebuilt many times.
Over the centuries, this sacred place has been visited by many a saint like श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.

-1847) and a host of others.
Śrīraṅgam is the largest temple-complex in India. Its area is 243 hectares (600 acres). The actual temple area is 62 hectares (2.5 sq. kms.).
The main temple is surrounded by seven concentric prākāras or boundary walls enclosing or housing several subsi-diary shrines as also the small township for the people living there.
The total number of gopuras (temple-towers) is 21.
The main deity is रङ्गनाथ, Lord विष्णु in the reclining posture. He is lying on Śeṣanāga or आदिशेष (the great serpent), forming the bed out of his coils and an umbrella of five hoods.
The image of रङ्गनाथ is 6.4 metres 21 ft.) long. Near his feet are seated भूदेवी and Nīlādevī, his consorts. In front of this original deity is kept the processional image or उत्सवमूर्ति. Another image called Tiruvaraṅga used as a substitute for worship during the period of Muslim invasions, is also kept in the sanctum.
The sanctum sanctorum is square inside and circular outside. Immediately round the altar, there is a circumambulatory passage used strictly for ritual purposes.
Encircling the sanctuary there is a moat-like canal of stone which is filled with water in summer to keep the sanctum cool.
On the upper wall there are paintings estimated to be 300 years old, depicting the 108 shrines dedicated to विष्णु and sacred to the Śrīvaiṣṇavas.
Above the main altar there is a Raṅgavimāna (a golden tower) containing carvings of four forms of विष्णु.
The outermost prākāra—the seventh in the series—has the main, most imposing gopuram, called the ‘Rājagopuram.’ completed and consecrated in A.

. It is 72 metres (235 ft.) high and has a passage below it which is 26 metres (100 ft.) long.
The area of this prākāra measures 864 metres by 742 metres (2880 ft. by 2475 ft.) The temple-tank is outside this prākāra. Houses and bazaars are situated in its enclosure.
The sixth prākāra houses the rathas or processional cars in its enclosure. The houses of the ब्राह्मणस् serving in the temples are also situated here.
The fifth prākāra-enclosure houses a museum apart from some temples.
From the enclosure of the fourth prākāra, the temple proper begins. This prākāra measures 370 metres by 254 metres (1235 ft. by 849 ft.). It contains a hall known as Garuḍamaṇḍapa with 212 pillars.
This prākāra itself has four gopurams in the four cardinal directions, the eastern one being the largest and the finest.
The other three enclosures created by the three prākāras are, naturally, smaller but contain several shrines.
It was Rāmānuja who reorganised the mode of worship in the temple (according to the Pāñcarātra Āgamas) and overhauled the entire administration. The same tradition has been kept up even now.
In this big temple-complex, there are several shrines dedicated to various aspects of विष्णु like हयग्रीव and कृष्ण, to the āyudhapuruṣas or the weapon-deities like सुदर्शन, Ālvārs, consorts of विष्णु and the ācāryas of the श्रीवैष्णव tradition, Rāmānuja, वेदान्त देशिक (A.

-1327).
One of the biggest attractions is the ‘thousand-pillared hall’ (150 metres by 48 metres or 500 ft. by 160 ft.) lying to the east in the inner campus. The actual number of granite pillars is 953 only, each being 5.4 metres (18 ft.) in height and intricately carved.
Out of the several festivals celebrated at the temple, the biggest is the वैकुण्ठ एकादशी (Puṣya-śuddha-एकादशी, the eleventh day in the bright fortnight of the month पुष्य, generally in December/ January). It is spread over twenty days. On this day, the उत्सवमूर्ति is gorgeously decorated, dressed in a garment of rubies and taken out in a magnificent procession to the thousand pillared hall.
The temple was attacked by the Muslim marauders from the north led by Malik Kāfur and Ulugh Khān in A.

. However, the devotees managed to save both the original deity and the processional icon.
Several kings and dynasties have helped in renovating as also maintaining this great temple. Some of them are: the Coḷas, the पल्लवस्, the Pāṇḍyas, the Hoysaḷas, the emperors of Vijayanagara and the Nāyaks of मदुरै.
There are as many as 600 inscriptions on the walls and other places in the complex.
There is a popular story and belief that शङ्कर (A.

-820) installed a Janākarṣakayantra (a special and sacred magical diagram) because of which this temple attracts a very large number of pilgrims and devotees, always, throughout the year.
The श्रीरङ्गम् temple is considered by a long-standing tradition to be one of the Navagrahasthala-temples (temples representing the nine प्लनेत्स्) and stands for the शुक्र or the Venus.
There is no doubt that this temple complex is a fortress that is protecting हिन्दुइस्म् in general and वैष्णविस्म् in particular.

Śrīśailam
(‘the holy hill’)
------------------------------------------
Śrīśailam—also called Śrīparvata—is a small town situated on the Ṛṣabhagiri hill, on the bank of the river Kṛṣṇā in the Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh.
The temple of शिव, known as Mallikārjuna, is the centre of attraction of this pilgrim centre. It is one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् (‘liṅgas of light’) known for their sanctity.
The deity gets this name because the original लिङ्ग used to be worshipped daily with mallikā or jasmine flowers.
The river, called locally as Pātālagaṅgā, is about 3 kms. down the hill. All the devotees who come for darśan (‘seeing [the लिङ्ग]’) must take a bath in this river.
The main temple is enclosed by a massive prākāra (boundary wall) which measures 183 metres by 152 metres (600 ft. by 500 ft.) and is 8.5 metres (29 ft.) high. It is made of huge blocks of stone riveted to one another.
On the inside of this prākāra, there are five regular rows of sculpture from above the base. There are innumerable varieties of figures of superb sculpture.
श्रीशैलम्">Mallikārjuna Temple at ŚrīśailamAccording to the earliest reference available in a Śātavāhana inscription the shrine existed even in the second century A. D. The temple however, has been renovated by several dynasties of kings who also gifted land and precious objects.
The गर्भगृह (sanctum) containing the लिङ्ग is a small stone-structure with an equally small pillared porch attached to the front. In front of this is the exquisitely carved मुखमण्डप or pillared hall built in A.

-1405 by the king हरिहर of Vijayanagara Empire. It contains several beautifully sculptured stone pillars and ornamental eaves, also of stone.
There is a नन्दि (the bull) near the eastern gateway.
All devotees, irrespective of their caste, creed or sex, are allowed inside the sanctum to touch the image and even bathe it with the water brought from the Pātālagaṅgā river.
The oldest structure in the campus is the shrine dedicated to Vṛddha-Mallikārjuna, assigned to the seventh century A. D. It is considered to be the original icon of the temple.
Under the Vaṭavṛkṣa (banyan tree) there is a small शिवलिङ्ग. The local legends say that this is the original शिवलिङ्ग upon which the black cow of the princess Candrāvatī who was living in that forest area at that time, used to empty her milk. The princess built a small temple to होउसे it, under instructions from शिव himself.
Other attractions within the prākāra are: the सहस्रलिङ्ग consisting of 1001 miniature liṅgas, established by Śrī राम on his way back from लङ्का; and five more liṅgas set up by the five Pāṇḍava princes in the inner courtyard.
The temple of Bhramarāmbā (Pārvatī) is outside the prākāra, above a flight of stairs.
A mirror hall to the right as one enters the gate and a beautiful icon of नटराज are the other attractions.
There is an Umāmaheśvara temple, about 3 kms. north-west of the Malli-kārjuna temple, on the way to the Pātālagaṅgā.
The main festival season is from February to the end of May, शिवरात्रि being the most important one.
The forest tribals known as Chenchus manage the temple through a जङ्गम priest.
Śrīśailam is a stronghold of the Vīra-śaivas or Liṅgāyats. It houses one of the five original monasteries. The stone liṅgas worn on the body by them are picked up from the bed of the Pātālagaṅgā river.

Introduction
The life of a god-man has two faces, the external and the internal. Whereas the former can be traced and described, the latter cannot be, since it is a matter of direct personal and mystical experience. श्रीकृष्ण Caitanya—also known as चैतन्य Mahāprabhu—belongs to this group.
Birth and Early Life
He was born on a full-मोओन् day (February 4, 1486) in the small town of Navadvīp (in Bengal) as the tenth child of Jagannātha Miśra and Śacīdevī. He was given the name Viśvambhara. His मोथेर् called him ‘Nimāi’ (the neem tree)—since she had lost eight children and the ninth had run away to become a monk—in the belief that the god of death would not touch him, he being ‘bitter’ like the neem leaves and fruits! Since his complexion was like that of gold and since he was extraordinarily handsome, he was given the name गौराङ्ग (the white one) also.
As a child, his pranks and naughty behaviour were very much reminiscent of those of श्रीकृष्ण himself. Certain unusual signs of divinity also—like demanding the ड़ोओद् offering meant for कृष्ण or humbling an elderly paṇḍit—started manifesting in him.
He was admitted into a Sanskrit school where he made astonishing progress in his एदुचतिओन् especially because of his exceedingly sharp intellect and memory.
Meanwhile his ड़थेर् passed away. मोथेर् शची took charge of his higher एदुचतिओन्. Very soon he matured into a great scholar of unsurpassed reputation. He also started his own ṭol (Sanskrit school). During this period he was married to लक्ष्मी, the daughter of a reputed paṇḍit, Vallbhācārya.
Being endowed with handsome features and immense scholarship, he now started on a tour of the nearby places to vanquish all the paṇḍits of the region and establish his supremacy over them all. When he returned he learnt that his wife had died of a snakebite. Maintaining his inner poise, he continued his teaching work at his ṭol. However his मोथेर् शची got him married to Viṣṇupriyā, the daughter of a wealthy paṇḍit of great reputation.
The Transformation
Some time after his tour, he decided to visit गया, the famous pilgrim centre of Gadādhara (Viṣṇu). During this visit, after he completed all the formal rituals he worshipped at the Viṣṇupāda (place containing the imprint of God’s foot-prints) where he had a strange mystical experience that changed his entire mood. He then begged ईश्वर पुरी (a saṁnyāsin-disciple of a well-known saint Mādha-vendra पुरी) whom he had known earlier and who was then present there, to initiate him into the मन्त्र of worship of कृष्ण, the beloved of the गोपीस्. ईश्वर पुरी obliged and Nimāi’s mood now changed completely into one of pathos (like that of the गोपीस्) due to an inner feeling of separation from कृष्ण, the beloved. Nimāi now became कृष्ण चैतन्य or चैतन्य Mahā-prabhu, the apostle of the love of कृष्ण.
Self-revelation
From now onwards, चैतन्य started going into ecstatic moods, his behaviour often making people doubt his sanity and mental balance. However, the great spiritual power that manifested in him now and then, totally transforming persons whom he touched, did also speak of the revelation of his divinity. Śrīvās, a committed devotee, अद्वैताचार्य the scholarly leader of the Vaiṣṇavas, Kāzi the Muslim Governor, Jagāi and Madhāi, the confirmed rowdies were some of the fortunate souls who gained from his infinite grace and compassion.
It was during this period that he gathered a good number of followers like Nityānanda or Nitāi who became his inseparable companion, Haridās (a Muslim saint), Murāri and others.
Adopting Saṁnyāsa
Caitanya now decided to take सṁन्यास (monastic life) and somehow managed to extract permission from his मोथेर् and wife. He then left Navadvīp and proceeded to Kaṭva where lived a great monk Keśava भारती, with whom he had had contacts earlier. Keśava भारती administered the monastic vows and changed his name to श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य.
Meanwhile his मोथेर् and the devotees met him and got the promise that he would live at Nīlācal (Jagannātha पुरी or पुरी) in Orissa (a nearby place) and not go to वृन्दाबन् (which is far off) as he had planned.
At Purī
This was his first visit to पुरी. The yearning to meet his कृष्ण at वृन्दाबन् now turned towards Jagannātha of पुरी, who was कृष्ण himself.
One of the important events that took place at पुरी was the चोन्वेर्सिओन् of वासुदेव Sārvabhauma, the doyen of scholars at that time, who was made to give up his Advaita philosophy and turn to devotion for Lord Kṛṣna.
Pilgrimages
Caitanya then undertook a long पिल्ग्रिमगे to South India (spread over two years) visiting all the important holy centres including कन्याकुमारी (in Tamil Nadu) and उडुपि (in Karnataka).
It was during this visit that he converted रामानन्द Roy, the governor of Vidyānagara (in Andhra Pradesh) under the king Pratāparudra of कलिङ्ग (Orissa), to the cult of devotion to कृष्ण. The king too, drawn by his magnetic personality, became his disciple.
After returning to पुरी and taking part in the famous रथयात्रा (car-festival) of Lord Jagannātha, he travelled towards वृन्दाबन् and returned via other holy places in North India like वाराणसी (Kāśī) and प्रयाग (Allahabad). It was during this tour that he made three important disciples Rūpa Gosvāmin (A.
-1558) and their nephew जीव Gosvāmin (d. A.

-1531) the well-known Vaiṣṇava teacher of the puṣṭimārga, met चैतन्य here.
Last Years
The last thirteen (or fourteen) years of life were spent by चैतन्य exclusively at पुरी. During this period he often used to be in ecstatic states of Kṛṣṇabhakti (as that of राधा towards कृष्ण). Hence someone had to be with him always to take care of him.
Though a great scholar, चैतन्य never left any writings of his own, except two exquisitely beautiful hymns—the Caitanyaśikṣāṣṭaka and the Jagannātha-stotra.
Apart from the Bhāgavata, चैतन्य was fond of the famous hymn Śrīkṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta and another work called the Brahmasaṁhitā.
The End
There are two versions of चैतन्य’s end. According to the first, he entered into the image of Jagannātha in the temple. The second account describes that he entered into the waters of the sea and disappeared.
Epilogue
Caitanya has been considered an इन्चर्नतिओन् of राधा and कृष्ण in one body. Though he exhibited in his life the intense love and passion of राधा for Kṛṣṇa—technically known as premābhakti—he led a very strict life as an ordained monk. There was absolutely no trace of काम or lust in his philosophy of devotion to कृष्ण or the राधा-कृष्ण ideal.
In course of time, वृन्दाबन् in the north, Navadvīp in Bengal in the east and पुरी in south-east became the centres of चैतन्य वैष्णविस्म्.
In Bengal, the Vaiṣṇava movement developed more as a चैतन्य cult than as a tradition of devotion to कृष्ण. A special contribution of this movement is the stress on kīrtans, singing of devotional songs to the accompaniment of musical instruments and dancing.
Inability of the common people to understand the significance of true devotion gradually gave rise to various unhealthy and immoral cults like those of the Sahajīyas, Kartābhajas, Vairāgi-Vairāgiṇīs and so on.

Śrīvidyā
(‘sacred or auspicious knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
If God can be conceived as the ड़थेर् in हेअवेन्, why not as the मोथेर् too? Human psychology being what it is, God has been approached or adored as the Divine मोथेर् also, not only in ancient India, but also in many other countries (See DEVĪ.).
One of the cults of the worship of देवी or the Divine मोथेर् is the श्रीविद्या. Literally, it means sacred or auspicious knowledge and is the same, for all practical purposes, as the ब्रह्मविद्या of the उपनिषद्स्.
In a more technical sense, it means upāsanā or the spiritual discipline connected with meditation and worship of the Divine मोथेर् in her aspect as ललिता-त्रिपुरसुन्दरी. The four mantras connected with it are also known by the same name.
They are: the Gāyatrīmantra; the pañcadaśākṣarīmantra; the षोडशाक्षरी-मन्त्र; and the bālātripurasundarī-मन्त्र.
Even among these, it is the pañca-daśākṣarīmantra (mantra of 15 letters) that is particularly called ‘Śrīvidyā’.
The basic treatises of श्रीविद्या are the following: Lalitāsahasranāma of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa with its commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara by Bhāskararāya Makhin (18th century A. D.); Lalitātriśatī, also from the same purāṇa, with a bhāṣya by शङ्कर (A.

-820); Nityaṣoḍa-śikārṇava (from the Vāmakeśvaratantra) with the commentary Setubandha by Bhaskararāya Makhin; Paraśurāma-kalpasūtra; Varivasyārahasya, also by Bhāskararāya Makhin.
The best known teachers of श्रीविद्या are the following: मनु, चन्द्र, कुबेर, लोपामुद्रा, मन्मथ, अगस्त्य, नन्दि-keśvara, सूर्य, विष्णु, शिव, स्कन्द and दुर्वासस्.
The श्रीविद्या, as a religio-spiritual system has three aspects: the philosophy, the ritual and the contemplation.
The Ultimate Reality is one in which there is a perfect merging of शिव (consciousness) and शक्ति (power). There arises in its मिन्द् the desire to become many. This is called विमर्श (deliberation). This creates स्पन्द (throb or stir) which develops into नाद (vibration), getting concentrated into a बिन्दु (point).
This बिन्दु gradually swells, giving rise to a polarisation of शिव (Father-principle) and शक्ति (Mother-principle), retaining at the same time the original latent and potent status containing the शिव-शक्ति combination. These three now form a triangle as it were. This process goes on getting repeated until it results in a pattern now well-known as the श्रीचक्र, representing the whole च्रेअतिओन्. (See ŚRĪCAKRA also.)
The ritual consists in the worship of the Śrīcakra—also known as Śrīyantra if it is in the form of a drawing, and मेरु, if a three-dimensional icon—with several items of worship. This is called ‘bahiryāga’.
As a continuation of the spiritual evolution brought about by the performance of a devoted बहिर्याग, ‘antaryāga’ results.
It is the spiritual contemplation of the श्रीचक्र as identified with the Divine मोथेर् ललिता-त्रिपुरसुन्दरी. At this stage, every act of the sādhaka (the worshipper) is elevated to the level of spiritual experience as depicted in the Saundaryalaharī (verse 27).
In tāntrik terminology, this entire process, which is in perfect harmony with the Vedic tradition, is called ‘Samayācāra’ (Samayā = देवी).
Repetition of the पञ्चदशाक्षरी-मन्त्र becomes an integral part of this अन्तर्याग.
This मन्त्र, as its very name indicates, has pañcadaśa (or fifteen) akṣaras (or letters). Unlike a word or a sentence comprising several letters of the alphabet giving some sensible meaning, these fifteen letters produce subtle vibrations revealing the subtle body or form of the goddess.
There are two versions of this मन्त्र, one beginning with the letter ka (hence called the ‘Kādimata’) attributed to the sage अगस्त्य and the other with the letter ha (hence termed ‘Hādimata’) promulgated by his wife लोपामुद्रा.
The only difference between these to versions is in the number of effective letters used.
(See मन्त्र">PAÑCADAŚĀKṢARĪ-MANTRA.)
Though there are several other versions of the मन्त्र, they are not very common.
The मन्त्र of the Kādimata is:
ka, e, ī, la, hrīṁ;
ha, sa, ka, ha, la, hrīm;
sa, ka, la, hrīm.
In the Hādimata, it is:
ha, sa, ka, la, hrīṁ;
ha, sa, ka, ha, la, hrīm;
sa, ka, la, hrīṁ.
Equally famous and very much in vogue is the ṣoḍaśīmantra, the मन्त्र with sixteen letters, got by adding śrīṁ at the end.
Another मन्त्र is the bālāmantra (aiṁ, klīṁ, sauḥ) which is addressed to the goddess as a bālā or a small girl.
In the Vedic as also the tāntrik tradition, every मन्त्र has a ṛṣi (seer), devatā (deity) and छन्दस् (metre). For the पञ्चदशाक्षरी-मन्त्र, दक्षिणामूर्ति (an aspect of शिव) is the ṛṣi. ललिता-त्रिपुरसुन्दरी is the devatā. Paṅkti is the छन्दस् (a Vedic metre with five syllables in each quarter).
The pañcadaśākṣarīmantra is divided into three kūṭas or parts each being given a separate name:
First part—Vāgbhavakūṭa.
Second part—Kāmarājakūṭa.
Third part—Śaktikūṭa.
These three represent the face, the torso and the legs (and feet) of the deity. Hence a devoted repetition of this मन्त्र helps in visualising the whole form of the deity.
Śrīvidyā is a highly esoteric science of spiritual wisdom. Hence it has to be received from an adept गुरु in a proper manner as described in the tāntrik works. Otherwise it can do more harm than good!

Śrīraṅgapaṭṭaṇa
------------------------------------------
Raṅganātha is an aspect of विष्णु. Images of रङ्गनाथ are invariably in the śayana or reclining posture. Three temples of this deity are at Śrīraṅga-paṭṭaṇa, Śivasamudra and श्रीरङ्गम्. The first two are in the Karnataka state and the last in Tamil Nadu. The deities are known as Ādiraṅga, Madhyaraṅga and Antyaraṅga respectively. All the three temples are situated on small islands created by the branching off into two, of the river कावेरी.
Śrīraṅgapaṭṭaṇa is a small town 13 kms. (8 miles) from the city of Mysore. According to the local legends, the great sage गौतम lived here and was worshipping the Ādiraṅga image. Tirumalayya, a chieftain of the kings of the Gaṅga race built the present temple in A.

and named the small town as Śrīraṅgapura.
The रङ्गनाथ temple has been built in the Dravidian style of architecture. At the entrance of the navaraṅga (open auditorium) there are two big images of Dvārapālakas (gate-keepers).
The original image is very beautiful and attractive. The serpent आदिशेष, on whom the deity is lying, has seven hoods. Near the feet of the deity is an image of goddess लक्ष्मी and of the sage गौतम.
There are two more temples in the town, of नरसिṁह (Man-lion इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) and of Gaṅgādhareśvara (Śiva) built during the 17th century A. D.
Very near श्रीरङ्गपट्टण is the pilgrim centre Paścimavāhinī. Here, one of the branches of the कावेरी river flows towards the west (= paścima) for a short distance. Hence the name. There are quite a few dharmaśālās (choultries) catering to the pilgrims who crowd here for the performance of religious rites.
